text: Feedback on research work has a different shape than a typical code review. A code review mostly asks whether the implementation does what it's supposed to, cleanly. Feedback on a research result has to engage with a messier question: is this conclusion actually supported by this evidence. This closing lesson covers how to give that kind of feedback usefully, and how to receive it without treating it as a personal critique.

The most useful research feedback takes the form of concrete, answerable questions rather than a vague expression of doubt: how many seeds, and what's the variance across them. Was the baseline given the same tuning budget as the treatment. And is there a confound — something other than the variable of interest that also differs between the two conditions being compared.

A reviewer can believe a hypothesis is plausible and still correctly flag that the specific experiment presented doesn't support it yet. 'I think sparsity probably helps, but one seed with no LR sweep for the sparse variant doesn't show that' isn't a rejection of the idea — it's a specific, answerable request for more seeds and an independent sweep.

The reframe that makes feedback productive on the receiving end: a reviewer poking at the evidence is doing exactly the job a researcher should want someone to do before a wrong conclusion gets reported or built upon. A request for another seed or a missing baseline is cheap next to the cost of a wrong conclusion propagating further.

That closes Chapter 7 — reports, negative results, project management, working with scientists, and now feedback, all aimed at making research conclusions ones a team can actually trust. Chapter 8 picks up from here with the handoff that moves a research result toward production, starting with handing off a research model.
